title: Pascals and mmHg: Why Blood Pressure Stayed Old-School
h1: Pascals and millimetres of mercury — the blood-pressure holdout
description: Every medical blood-pressure reading is in mmHg. SI would say kPa. Here is why medicine kept mmHg and how the two convert.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against ISO 81060-1 and JNC 8 guidelines

hero: 120/80 mmHg is 16.0/10.7 kPa. Medicine keeps mmHg because the original instruments were literal mercury columns — and the number scale is too familiar to change.
body: Every clinical blood-pressure guideline in the world is written in mmHg. The pascal-based equivalent (kPa) is technically correct but has never displaced the mercury column, which was the physical measurement device until digital cuffs took over in the 2000s.

> 1 mmHg = 133.322 Pa (near-exact for mercury at 0°C, standard g)
> 1 kPa = 7.500 mmHg
> 120 mmHg = 15.999 kPa
> 80 mmHg = 10.666 kPa
> 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa

The Riva-Rocci sphygmomanometer (1896) used a mercury column because mercury's density (13,595 kg/m³) makes a manageable-sized instrument — 760 mm reads 1 atmosphere. A water column reading the same pressure would be 10.3 m tall. Medicine standardised around the mercury column, and the unit outlived the device.

Digital cuffs use piezoresistive pressure sensors, calibrated in kPa internally, then displayed in mmHg for clinician familiarity. WHO discourages mercury sphygmomanometers over environmental toxicity concerns, but a majority of clinical trials since 2000 still report readings in mmHg because comparability with historical data demands it.

140 mmHg × 0.1333 = 18.67 kPa systolic. 90 mmHg × 0.1333 = 12.00 kPa diastolic. Pulse pressure = 50 mmHg = 6.67 kPa. Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic + 1/3 × pulse pressure = 90 + 16.7 = 106.7 mmHg = 14.2 kPa. Every calculation works in either unit — clinicians just prefer the historical scale.

Intraocular pressure: mmHg (normal 10–21). Cerebrospinal fluid pressure: mmH₂O or cmH₂O (10 mmH₂O = 0.736 mmHg). Ventilator peak airway pressure: cmH₂O. Central venous pressure: mmHg or cmH₂O depending on hospital tradition. Each specialty picked its own convention decades ago.
1 mmHg = 133 Pa. 120/80 = 16.0/10.7 kPa. Medicine stays with mmHg because every guideline and every trial does. Digital cuffs display it internally translated.

faqs.q: Why isn't torr used in medicine?
faqs.a: 1 torr = 1 mmHg to 6 significant figures, so 'torr' and 'mmHg' are interchangeable. Physics uses torr; medicine uses mmHg. Same number.
A minority (Netherlands, Scandinavia) report BP in kPa. Most European medicine follows global convention: mmHg.
Not systematically. Cardiovascular BP responds to acute hypoxia (increased sympathetic tone) but returns to baseline over weeks of acclimatisation.
